title: Policy as code on the plan
summary: Rules that read the plan JSON and block a pull request: Open Policy Agent with conftest, Sentinel and OPA policy sets in HCP Terraform, enforcement levels, and writing the team's first rules.

steps.title: Rules a reviewer should not have to remember
body: Some rules hold for every change: no public buckets, no `0.0.0.0/0` on port 22, no destroying databases from CI,
every resource tagged with an owner. Reviewers miss them at 6 p.m. **Policy as code** checks them on the plan JSON
(`terraform show -json tfplan`), which has the *final* values after variables, modules and functions.
```rego
# policy/plan.rego, checked with: conftest test plan.json --policy policy/
package main
import rego.v1
protected := {"aws_db_instance", "aws_s3_bucket"}
deny contains msg if {
some rc in input.resource_changes
rc.type in protected
"delete" in rc.change.actions          # a destroy, or the destroy half of a replacement
msg := sprintf("%s would be destroyed: needs a manual, approved change", [rc.address])
Where policies run:
- **OPA** (Open Policy Agent, a CNCF project) with **conftest** in any CI, for Terraform and OpenTofu alike.
- **HCP Terraform / Terraform Enterprise** run **Sentinel** or **OPA** policy sets between plan and apply, with
enforcement levels: *advisory* (warn), *soft-mandatory* (an authorised person may override), *hard-mandatory*.
- Terraform 1.17 also made **Terraform Policy** generally available: `terraform plan -policies=...` evaluates policies
in the CLI itself.
- Static scanners (Checkov, Trivy's misconfiguration scanning) read the `.tf` files instead of the plan: faster, but
blind to values computed from variables and modules.

steps.prompt: Why check the **plan JSON** rather than grep the `.tf` files for `0.0.0.0/0`?
options: The plan has the final values after variables, locals, modules and functions; the CIDR may come from a tfvars file or a module default the grep never sees
`.tf` files cannot be read by OPA
steps.explain: `cidr_blocks = var.allowed_cidrs` looks harmless in the code; the plan shows `["0.0.0.0/0"]`. Plan-based policy also sees the *actions*: whether something is created, changed or destroyed.

steps.title: The team's first two rules
prompt: `~/infra/policy-demo/plans/` has the JSON of two real plans: `safe.json` (changes a message) and `bad.json` (a pull
request that rotates the DB password, drops the API key and makes a file world-writable). Write
1. no `random_password` or `tls_private_key` may be destroyed or replaced (`"delete"` in its actions). The message
2. no `local_file` may end up world-writable: deny when `rc.change.after.file_permission` is `"0666"` or `"0777"`
`conftest test plans/bad.json -p policy` must fail with three messages; `plans/safe.json` must pass. Explore the

checks.name: the bad plan is refused, for the right reasons
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/policy-demo && ! conftest test plans/bad.json -p policy --no-color > /tmp/o 2>&1; grep -q 'random_password.db' /tmp/o && grep -q 'tls_private_key.api' /tmp/o && grep -q 'local_file.motd' /tmp/o && grep -q '3 failures' /tmp/o
checks.fail: `conftest test plans/bad.json -p policy` should fail with exactly three messages, naming `random_password.db`, `tls_private_key.api` and `local_file.motd`.

checks.name: the safe plan passes
checks.fail: `conftest test plans/safe.json -p policy` should pass: changing a file's content (with 0644) is allowed.

checks.name: the rules are in plan.rego
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/policy-demo && grep -q '^package main' policy/plan.rego && test "$(grep -c 'deny contains' policy/plan.rego)" -ge 2
checks.fail: `policy/plan.rego` should be `package main` with (at least) two `deny contains msg if { ... }` rules.

hints: Rule 1 is the card's rule with `protected := {"random_password", "tls_private_key"}`.
Rule 2: `some rc in input.resource_changes`, `rc.type == "local_file"`, `rc.change.after.file_permission in {"0666", "0777"}`, then `msg := sprintf(...)`.
Run `conftest test plans/bad.json -p policy` after each rule. A destroyed resource has `after = null`, so rule 2 only fires on files that will exist.
solution: msg := sprintf("%s would be destroyed or replaced: rotate secrets with an approved change", [rc.address])
msg := sprintf("%s would be world-writable (%s)", [rc.address, rc.change.after.file_permission])
steps.explain: Three failures: the password (replaced), the key (destroyed) and the file. In CI this step runs right after `terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json`, and its messages are posted on the pull request. Policies are code too: `conftest verify` runs unit tests for them (`test_` rules with sample inputs), and they live in a repo with their own reviews.

steps.prompt: Match the enforcement level (HCP Terraform policy sets) to what happens when a policy fails.
pairs: the run continues, with a warning
the run stops unless an authorised user overrides it
the run stops; nobody can override

steps.prompt: A policy denies destroying `aws_db_instance`. The team really must replace a database once (a planned migration). What is the healthy way?
options: An explicit, reviewed exception: a soft-mandatory override by an authorised person, or an allow-list entry for that one address in the policy repo
Run `terraform apply` from a laptop to skip CI
Delete the policy and add it back later
Use `-target` so the policy does not see it
steps.explain: Guard rails should make the dangerous path deliberate and recorded, not impossible. Every bypass that is easier than the approved exception will become the normal way.
